title: Krishna Speaks for the Silent Disguised Brothers
story:
The king of Magadha had done everything a host should do. He had risen in haste when the three Brahmanas were brought before him, and he had received them with water to wash their feet, with honey and the other ingredients of the Arghya, with gifts of kine, and with every other form of respect his court could offer. "Ye are welcome," the great king said.

And both of his two younger guests remained silent.

The king had come to this meeting in a season of ill omens. The learned Brahmanas of Girivraja had seen many evil signs and reported them to him, and Jarasandha, to ward off the evils, had entered upon the celebration of a sacrifice with proper vows and fasts, his priest making him mount an elephant and whirling lighted brands about him. The broken mountain had promised him trouble; now three strangers stood where the trouble had arrived, and one of them was about to speak for all three.

The moment stretched. The three strangers had passed along the public road of the capital, past the shops full of various edibles and floral wreaths, supplied with articles of every variety that man can desire, and had snatched forcibly from the flower-vendors the garlands they had exposed for sale — as if the city itself were already theirs to help themselves from. The people of Magadha had wondered at them: heroes looking like elephants, with necks broad like those of trees and wide chests, their arms, besmeared with sandal paste, like the trunks of sala trees. Passing through three gates crowded with men, proudly and cheerfully they had come at last to the king. Now they stood before him, and his welcome had fallen into a silence he had not expected.

Krishna spoke for the three of them. "O king of kings," he said, "these two are now in the observance of a vow. Therefore they will not speak. Silent they will remain till midnight. After that hour they will speak with thee."

The explanation was simple and absolute. The king had received guests who could not answer him: not a single word until the hour of midnight, when the vow would end. Whatever questions Jarasandha might have wished to ask — who these Brahmanas were, whence they had come, what errand had brought them to the capital of Magadha — would have to wait for the night hour, and for the guests themselves to choose the moment their silence broke.

Until then, they were simply guests under his roof, owing him nothing but their presence while the hours of the night ran down. The court of Girivraja settled into waiting. The king had offered his welcome; the vow had answered for the two silent brothers; and the first words between Jarasandha and the disguised trio would come only when midnight released them.
reflection: A vow of silence was a clever shield: it let Krishna's party enter the enemy's court, accept its honours, and give away nothing — not a word, not a name — until the hour they themselves chose. Jarasandha's hospitality was turned into a waiting game, and the waiting belonged to the host.
next_story_tease: When midnight came, Jarasandha would question the strangers about their disguise.
hero_scene: In the court of Girivraja, Jarasandha stands with raised arms in welcome while two silent, garlanded Brahmana guests stand motionless beside Krishna, who alone speaks, addressing the king — the whole court held in the tension of the unexplained silence.
visual_elements: Krishna speaking while Bhima and Arjuna stand silent
the trio's bright robes, garlands, and ear-rings
the water, honey, and Arghya of the welcome
